extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants (Korea, KIPO)
extracted.subtask_description: Examination rules and substantive patentability standards used by the Korean Intellectual Property Office, covering deposits of microorganisms, sequence listing requirements, and statutory patentability criteria such as industrial applicability and novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit certificate requirement for microorganisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application for which a micro-organism is to be deposited includes the fact of deposit and the deposit number, but not a copy of the deposit certificate, an examiner shall consider that the micro-organism is not deposited and conduct examination on the application. However, where an applicant failed to attach a copy of the deposit certificate and then attach the copy of the deposit certificate after being notified of a ground for rejection from an examiner, the examiner shall accept the copy and conduct examination on the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If certificate is missing at filing treat as not deposited; acceptance permitted if certificate submitted after a rejection notification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment disclosing deposit number is new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the original specification of an application where a micro-organism is to be deposited did not state the deposit number and then the number is disclosed through amendment, it shall be deemed to be the addition of new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding a deposit number by amendment to an original specification that did not include it is treated as introducing new matter (prohibited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Name change after deposit/classification adjustment — evidential document rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a micro-organism is deposited and the deposit certificate is attached before filing and relevant facts such as deposit numbers in the specification, but the patent classification of the deposited micro-organism is adjusted and then its name is changed, if a copy of the evidential document issued by a depository institution is submitted, it shall not be deemed to be the addition of new matter even though an amendment of changing the name of the concerned micro-organisms is made. However, where the scientific characteristic of the concerned micro-organism of the newly-adjusted patent classification which is not disclosed in the original specification is stated, it shall be deemed to be the addition of new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name changes supported by an evidential document from the depository are acceptable unless they introduce new scientific characteristics not in the original specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of microorganism deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposit of micro-organisms shall be completed by the time of filing the application. The time of the deposit of micro-organisms shall be deemed to be the date when the applicant deposits the concerned micro-organisms to a depository institution and then the depository institution receives the micro-organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposit must have been completed by filing date (defined as applicant deposit + depository receipt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to submit deposit certificate after disclosing deposit number
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the applicant filed an application by only disclosing the deposit number on the specification and failed to submit the deposit certificate through amendment even after filing the application, it shall be deemed that the deposit has never been made on the date of deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely stating a deposit number without submitting the certificate (and failing to later submit it) is treated as if no deposit occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalities check for microorganism deposit (pre-2015/ post-2015 distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications filed after January 1, 2015, formalities examination should check whether microorganism stated in the proving documents is deposited before filing a patent application. Where proving documents are attached without indicating an intention of filing the application or vice versa, this contravenes rules and amendments shall be proposed under Article 46; failure to remedy may invalidate deposit-related proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform formalities checks of proving documents and intention to file; propose Article 46 amendments for deficiencies; persistent deficiencies can invalidate deposit proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deficiencies in deposit details must be communicated and remedied
rubrics_metrics.description: Where microorganism is not deposited before filing, or the name of the depositary authority, the depositary number and the depositary date are incorrectly stated in the patent application and the proving documents, the deficiencies shall be communicated to the patent applicant and be proposed to remedy. Where the deficiencies are not remedied in response to the amendment proposal within a time limit specified, a proceeding related to the deposit of micro-organisms can be invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should notify deficiencies and request amendments; non-response within time limit may lead to invalidation of deposit proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination conditional on deposit/formalities correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there are no deficiencies identified in the documents submitted by a patent applicant, substantive examination shall be conducted. As for a patent application for which deposit of microorganism is required, where the depositary number is stated in the specification or drawing(s) originally attached but the intention of filing an application involving microorganism is neither stated nor deficiencies remedied, a proceeding related to the deposit can be invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive examination proceeds only after formalities are satisfied; unresolved formal defects concerning deposit can lead to invalidation and use of Article 42(3)(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositary number indication format
rubrics_metrics.description: The indication of depositary number by depositary authority shall follow specified formats (table of Patent Micro-organism / Domestic Deposit / Int’l Deposit / General Deposit with KCTC, KCCM, KCLRF, KACC variants and formats like 'KCTC No.P', 'KCTC No.BP', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should require depositary numbers to be indicated according to the prescribed authority-specific formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement for microorganism inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for a person skilled in the art to practice an invention of microorganism, the specification should: (①) where a person can easily get microorganism, in detail establish the process of obtaining the final product microorganism from starting material together with the process of getting microorganism; ② where a person cannot easily get microorganism and it is difficult to establish the process in the description, the embodiment can be supported by depositing the final product microorganism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either provide a detailed process enabling practice by a skilled person or deposit the final microorganism; without deposit, a detailed process in the description may still support the embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence listing inclusion requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who intends to file a patent application including nucleic acid sequence or amino acid sequence shall include the sequence list written according to the method decided by the Commissioner of the KIPO in the specification and attach the electronic file containing the sequence list drawn in the method set by the Commissioner. However, where the sequence list drawn according to the method is disclosed in the specification in the electronic form, the electronic file does not need to be attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence lists must follow the Commissioner's prescribed method and be attached as an electronic file unless the spec itself contains the electronic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence list detailed method and directive
rubrics_metrics.description: Details regarding the method of writing sequence list and electronic file of sequence list shall be based on the guideline for writing nucleic acid sequence or amino acid sequence (KIPO Directive No. 2013-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow KIPO Directive No.2013-1 for format and content of sequence lists and electronic files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedence when sequence lists differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the sequence list disclosed in the specification and the sequence list contained in the electronic file are different, the examiner shall examine the application based on the sequence list disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If discrepancy exists between spec and electronic file, the printed/specification-disclosed sequence list controls examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment rules apply mutatis mutandis to sequence lists
rubrics_metrics.description: The examination guideline regarding sequence lists shall apply mutatis mutandis to amendments to the sequence list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence list amendment handling follows same procedural rules as original sequence list requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing sequence list — enablement rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention disclosed in claims cannot be easily practiced because the sequence list is not disclosed in the specification, an examiner shall notify a ground for rejection under Article 42(3)(i) of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to include a required sequence list that prevents enablement should lead to a rejection under Article 42(3)(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing electronic sequence file — formality amendment or invalidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the electronic file of the sequence list is not attached in the application (except where the sequence list is disclosed in the specification in electronic form), this shall be subject to amendment because of violation of the method set by orders under the Patent Act. The examiner shall request an amendment under Article 46 and if irregularities are not addressed, invalidate the application proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request Article 46 amendment for missing electronic sequence file; persistent failure leads to invalidation. Note: image-scanned sequence lists are not acceptable as the electronic file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image-scanned sequence list not acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: The image-scanned sequence list is not the electronic file of sequence list drawn by the method set by the Commissioner of the KIPO. Therefore, where the image-scanned sequence list is attached, the examiner shall treat it as if the electronic file of sequence list is not attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject scanned images as substitute for the required electronic sequence file; require proper electronic file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability requirement (Article 29)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention having industrial applicability is patentable, other than inventions publicly known or practiced or published or made available to the public via telecommunications lines prior to the filing of a patent application (Article 29).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial applicability is a threshold for patentability; prior public disclosure/practice/publication are exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad interpretation of 'industry'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'industry' shall be interpreted in a broad sense to cover all useful activities and practical technologies (Paris Convention Article 1(3) referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a broad conception of industry when assessing industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory invention — use of laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is defined as the creation of a technical idea using the laws of nature; laws of nature as such (e.g., second law of thermodynamics) are not statutory inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude pure laws of nature from statutory inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere discoveries vs isolated/artificially obtained natural things
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere discovery is not a creation and thus not statutory. However, if things in nature are isolated artificially from their surroundings, the methods, isolated chemical substances or microorganisms are considered statutory inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation or artificial derivation of natural things can render them patent-eligible; mere discovery of natural phenomena is excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: New use of known material — non-statutory unless inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: A use invention claiming a new use of a known material is generally non-statutory, but if the new use is closely related, with non-obvious inventive activities, to the newly found property, the use invention may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inventive contribution of new use linked to newly found property rather than automatically excluding all new-use claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions contrary to laws of nature excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Those contrary to laws of nature (e.g., perpetual motion) are not considered statutory inventions because an invention must utilize a law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude claims that require means contrary to established physical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-technical subject matter exclusion and technical effect exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed invention uses laws other than laws of nature (economic laws, mathematical methods, logics, cartography, mental activities), arbitrary arrangements, or mental activities, the claimed invention is not statutory. However, where data processing or methods are specifically executed using hardware or give useful, concrete and tangible results by increasing or controlling performance of technical tools, they may be deemed statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a technical device or technical effect (concrete/tangible result) to transform an otherwise non-statutory abstract method into statutory subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal skill exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal skill acquired by personal practice cannot be shared with third parties as knowledge due to lack of objectivity, so it is not considered a statutory invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude claims that are merely individual skills (e.g., performing musical instruments) from patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere presentation of information exclusion and exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere presentation of information where the technical feature resides solely in the content of the information and its main objective is to present the information is not statutory. However, if the technical feature resides in the presentation per se, the means for presentation or the method for presentation, it might be considered statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish content-only information presentations from inventions where presentation means/format provide technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic creation exclusion and technical-composition exception
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetic creation itself (e.g., paintings, carvings as such) is not statutory, but if achieved by technical composition or other technical means, they may be viewed as statutory inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether technical measures contribute to the aesthetic creation sufficiently to render it statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer program / computer-implemented invention treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer program alone is not considered a statutory invention. However, inventions where data processing is specifically executed using hardware, a data processing unit operating with the program, its operating method, a computer-readable medium carrying the program, and the computer program stored in medium (applied to applications filed on and after July 1, 2014) are considered statutory inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After July 1, 2014, examine computer-implemented inventions for hardware-specific implementation or technical effect to determine statutory status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility/outcome achievable requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention whose outcome of the claimed subject matter is not achievable and reproducible is not considered statutory even if means are sufficiently described. Possibility less than 100% is acceptable if outcome is certain to be achievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require a reasonable assurance of reproducibility/achievability; absolute 100% is not required but outcome must be demonstrably achievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness requirement and amendment limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A statutory invention shall be complete: subject matters must be specified clearly and thoroughly so a person skilled in the art may easily reproduce the invention. An incomplete invention at filing cannot be amended later to correct the defect; deficiency in description in an otherwise complete invention may be corrected by amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate incomplete inventions (non-amendable) from descriptive deficiencies (amendable); prefer to notify rejection under Article 42(3)(i) when unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of grounds for rejection for non-statutory inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application falls under non-statutory inventions (law of nature, discovery, subject matters against law of nature, non-use of law of nature, mere presentation of information, aesthetic creations, incomplete invention), the ground for rejection shall be notified with the ground that the invention does not involve 'inventions that have industrial applicability', citing Article 29(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Article 29(1) main paragraph in rejection notices for non-statutory subject matter and be as specific as possible in reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model vs patent subject-matter distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Utility Model Act, a utility model may be granted only for utility innovations that relate to the shape or construction of an article or a combination of articles, whereas the Patent Act allows product (including composition) and method claims. If an independent claim is a utility innovation regarding shape or construction and dependent claims define a material, the dependent claim may be considered statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claimed subject matter better fits utility model regime (shape/construction) or patent regime (methods/compositions) and treat dependent claims accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical practice exclusion (industrial inapplicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method for treatment of the human body by surgery or therapy and diagnostic methods practiced on the human body are considered industrially inapplicable inventions. A method including medical activities even as part of the whole step or as indispensable parts in claims is not industrially applicable. Methods whose purpose is both therapeutic and non-therapeutic (e.g., cosmetic effects) or where therapeutic vs non-therapeutic effects cannot be separated are inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude clinical treatment and diagnostic methods practiced on humans; distinguish measurement/data-collection methods that do not involve clinical judgment (these may be applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical device and sample-analysis applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: A medical device to be used in operations on the human body or for cure/diagnosis and medical products are classified as industrially applicable. A method for operating a medical device or a measurement method with the device (when the device is newly invented) is considered industrially applicable except when it includes clinical medical activities. Methods for treating/analyzing samples extracted from the human body or gathering data by analyzing such samples are considered industrially applicable when separable from medical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Device claims and ex-vivo sample analysis claims may be patentable even if in the medical field; ensure steps are separable from direct clinical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal-only limitation may render medical method applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a method could be used for treatment of the human body, it is considered industrially applicable if the method is limited to be practiced on the animal body excluded from being practiced on a human body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims explicitly limited to non-human animals can avoid medical-practice exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business-use / marketability requirement for industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention only for personal use, academic or experimental purposes is regarded as industrially inapplicable. An invention concerning marketable or tradable subject matter is considered industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the invention has potential commercial/industrial application beyond purely personal or research uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practically impossible inventions are industrially inapplicable
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention which cannot be implemented or practiced is not industrially applicable even if it works in theory (example: covering the whole earth's surface with an ultraviolet-absorbing film).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject inventions that are clearly impracticable; future applicability is acceptable if realistic, but not merely speculative based on possible future tech advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty exclusions — public knowledge/practice/publication/telecommunications
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention publicly known or practiced, published in a publication, or made available to the public via telecommunications lines prior to filing is not novel and thus not patentable (Article 29).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty against any public disclosure or practice anywhere prior to exact filing time (file time considered to hour/minute converted to Korean time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly known' for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Publicly known' means contents known to an unspecified person without obligation of secrecy in Korea or a foreign country prior to filing. The time of filing refers to the exact filing moment (hour and minute). 'Unspecified persons' refers to general public not bound by secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a stringent temporal standard (exact filing moment) and consider whether knowledge was accessible to the general public without secrecy obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly practiced' for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Publicly practiced' means an invention practiced under conditions where the contents are publicly known or can potentially be publicly known. Even where a small part of technical features is kept secret, it may still be publicly practiced. Example: observing production at a plant exposed to unspecified persons may render an invention publicly practiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether practice of an invention made its content observable/knowable to unspecified persons; potential exposure can suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior application/publication as prior art — publication and public inspection nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application is not laid open and is not published after registration, the invention shall not be used as prior art under Article 29(1)(2). However, after decision of registration, if the application is made available for public inspection, it may be used as prior art under Article 20(1)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish unpublished/unavailable filings from those made publicly available by publication or public inspection when assessing novelty.
